title: The power of humans: Ozymandias, London, My Last Duchess and Tissue
specPoints: Paper 2 Section B: Power and Conflict: Ozymandias, London, My Last Duchess, Tissue

tips.title: Four powers, four endings
tips.body: Ozymandias: nothing remains. London: the marriage hearse. My Last Duchess: another possession. Tissue: paper turned into skin.

tips.title: Voice is the method
tips.body: Reported (Ozymandias), a walking witness (London), a dramatic monologue (My Last Duchess), a reflective extended metaphor (Tissue).

tips.title: Four dates to carry
tips.body: London 1794, Ozymandias 1818, My Last Duchess 1842, Tissue 2006.

tips.title: Best pairs
tips.body: Ozymandias with My Last Duchess for tyrants; London with Tissue for power written into things.

why.matters: These four poems ask what power is made of and what undoes it: a statue, a city's rules, a husband's commands, lines on a map. Each gives power a different voice, and learning how voice and form shape what the reader thinks of that power is the heart of AO2. They also pair well with each other and with the war poems, so they widen the choices in the exam.

examples.title: The statue that falls
examples.body: Statues of rulers are pulled down when regimes change, and the photographs go round the world. Ozymandias imagined the same scene two centuries earlier: the boast still on the pedestal, the power gone.

examples.title: A line on a map
examples.body: Borders drawn by people on paper decide where millions can live and work, and they are redrawn after wars. Tissue asks how strong such lines really are, when the sun shines through them.

steps.title: Ozymandias: power against time
steps.body:
Percy Bysshe Shelley published *Ozymandias* in 1818. Ozymandias is a Greek name for the Egyptian pharaoh Ramesses II. Shelley was a radical who hated tyranny, and the poem is a sonnet about what time does to a tyrant.

> I met a traveller from an antique land\
> Who said: Two vast and trunkless legs of stone\
> Stand in the desert...Near them, on the sand,\
> Half sunk, a shattered visage lies, whose frown,\
> And wrinkled lip, and sneer of cold command,\
> Tell that its sculptor well those passions read\
> Which yet survive, stamped on these lifeless things,\
> The hand that mocked them, and the heart that fed:\
> And on the pedestal these words appear:\
> ‘My name is Ozymandias, king of kings:\
> Look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair!’\
> Nothing beside remains. Round the decay\
> Of that colossal wreck, boundless and bare\
> The lone and level sands stretch far away.

**Told at a distance.** “I met a traveller from an antique land”: the speaker reports a traveller, who describes a statue, made by a sculptor, of a king. The layers of report push the king further and further away.

**The face.** “a shattered visage”, a frown and “sneer of cold command”: the sculptor read the king's passions truly, and his art has outlived the man.

**The irony.** The inscription boasts “Look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair!”, and then “Nothing beside remains.” The Mighty should despair, but not for the reason he meant.

visuals.alt: Four boxes on Ozymandias: the reported voice, the king, the boast, and the answer of the desert

check.prompt: What is the irony of Look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair!?
check.solution: The boast was meant to crush other kings with envy. Surrounded by empty sand, it tells them to despair that all power ends like this. The words are the same; time has changed their meaning.

markScheme.description: He meant rivals to despair at his power; now they should despair because even his works have gone

options: He meant rivals to despair at his power; now they should despair because even his works have gone
That the king was not mighty at all, because the statue was very small and the traveller could hardly see it in the desert, which is why the sculptor made the face so large
That the king was a kind ruler
There is no irony

steps.title: London: a city in chains
steps.body:
William Blake's *London* appeared in *Songs of Experience* in 1794, five years after the French Revolution began, when radical ideas were feared in Britain.

> I wander through each chartered street,\
>  Near where the chartered Thames does flow,\
> A mark in every face I meet,\
>  Marks of weakness, marks of woe.
>
> In every cry of every man,\
>  In every infant’s cry of fear,\
> In every voice, in every ban,\
>  The mind-forged manacles I hear:
>
> How the chimney-sweeper’s cry\
>  Every blackening church appals,\
> And the hapless soldier’s sigh\
>  Runs in blood down palace-walls.
>
> But most, through midnight streets I hear\
>  How the youthful harlot’s curse\
> Blasts the new-born infant’s tear,\
>  And blights with plagues the marriage hearse.

**Chartered.** “I wander through each chartered street”: charters granted rights of ownership, so even the streets and the river belong to someone. The speaker walks through a city that is owned.

**Repetition.** “Marks of weakness, marks of woe”; “In every cry of every man”: *every* is repeated until the suffering is total.

**The chains are in the mind.** “The mind-forged manacles I hear”: people are bound by ideas, by fear and habit, as much as by power.

**Institutions.** The chimney-sweeper's cry shames the church, “Every blackening church appals”; “And the hapless soldier's sigh Runs in blood down palace-walls”. The poem ends on an oxymoron: “And blights with plagues the marriage hearse”.

rows: The city owned, even the river
Marks of weakness, marks of woe
Love and death in one image
props.title: London in four lines

visuals.alt: A table of four lines from London and what each does

check.prompt: What does the mind-forged manacles suggest?
check.solution: Manacles are handcuffs; mind-forged means made in the mind. Blake's radical claim is that power works through what people believe, which is harder to break than iron.

markScheme.description: People are imprisoned by their own ideas and the ideas imposed on them, not only by physical chains

options: That the people of London have been arrested and chained by the police for taking part in riots during the French Revolution, which Blake saw from his window in 1794
People are imprisoned by their own ideas and the ideas imposed on them, not only by physical chains
That Blake worked as a blacksmith
That the city has too many prisons

steps.title: My Last Duchess: power that speaks
steps.body:
Robert Browning published *My Last Duchess* in 1842. It is a dramatic monologue: one character speaks to a silent listener, and the reader learns more than the speaker means to tell. The speaker is a Renaissance Duke of Ferrara; the listener is the envoy of a Count whose daughter the Duke means to marry.

> That's my last Duchess painted on the wall,\
> Looking as if she were alive. I call\
> That piece a wonder, now: Fra Pandolf's hands\
> Worked busily a day, and there she stands.\
> Will't please you sit and look at her? I said\
> "Fra Pandolf" by design: for never read\
> Strangers like you that pictured countenance,\
> The depth and passion of its earnest glance,\
> But to myself they turned (since none puts by\
> The curtain I have drawn for you, but I)\
> And seemed as they would ask me, if they durst,\
> How such a glance came there; so, not the first\
> Are you to turn and ask thus. Sir, 'twas not\
> Her husband's presence only, called that spot\
> Of joy into the Duchess' cheek: perhaps\
> Fra Pandolf chanced to say "Her mantle laps\
> Over my lady's wrist too much," or "Paint\
> Must never hope to reproduce the faint\
> Half-flush that dies along her throat:" such stuff\
> Was courtesy, she thought, and cause enough\
> For calling up that spot of joy. She had\
> A heart--how shall I say?--too soon made glad,\
> Too easily impressed; she liked whate'er\
> She looked on, and her looks went everywhere.\
> Sir, 'twas all one! My favour at her breast,\
> The dropping of the daylight in the West,\
> The bough of cherries some officious fool\
> Broke in the orchard for her, the white mule\
> She rode with round the terrace--all and each\
> Would draw from her alike the approving speech,\
> Or blush, at least. She thanked men,--good! but thanked\
> Somehow--I know not how--as if she ranked\
> My gift of a nine-hundred-years-old name\
> With anybody's gift. Who'd stoop to blame\
> This sort of trifling? Even had you skill\
> In speech--(which I have not)--to make your will\
> Quite clear to such an one, and say, "Just this\
> Or that in you disgusts me; here you miss,\
> Or there exceed the mark"--and if she let\
> Herself be lessoned so, nor plainly set\
> Her wits to yours, forsooth, and made excuse,\
> --E'en then would be some stooping: and I choose\
> Never to stoop. Oh, sir, she smiled, no doubt,\
> Whene'er I passed her; but who passed without\
> Much the same smile? This grew; I gave commands;\
> Then all smiles stopped together. There she stands\
> As if alive. Will't please you rise? We'll meet\
> The company below, then. I repeat,\
> The Count your master's known munificence\
> Is ample warrant that no just pretence\
> Of mine for dowry will be disallowed;\
> Though his fair daughter's self, as I avowed\
> At starting, is my object. Nay, we'll go\
> Together down, sir. Notice Neptune, though,\
> Taming a sea-horse, thought a rarity,\
> Which Claus of Innsbruck cast in bronze for me!

**Control.** “That's my last Duchess painted on the wall”; he keeps it behind “The curtain I have drawn for you”. The Duchess is now an object he owns and shows.

**His complaint.** She had “A heart--how shall I say?--too soon made glad”; she thanked men as if they ranked with “My gift of a nine-hundred-years-old name”. He would not correct her: “and I choose Never to stoop”.

**The chill.** “I gave commands; Then all smiles stopped together”. He does not say what the commands were, and does not need to.

visuals.alt: Four boxes on the Duke in My Last Duchess: the voice, control, pride, and threat

check.prompt: What does the Duke imply with I gave commands; Then all smiles stopped together?
check.solution: The line is deliberately vague and completely clear. Her smiles went to everyone; he gave commands; the smiles stopped. The envoy, and the reader, understand what kind of man is choosing a new wife.

markScheme.description: That he had the Duchess killed, or silenced, because her smiles were not kept for him alone

options: That he told a joke
That he asked the servants to stop laughing in the palace because it disturbed him when he was working on his collection of paintings and bronze statues from Innsbruck
That he had the Duchess killed, or silenced, because her smiles were not kept for him alone
That the Duchess stopped smiling because she was ill

steps.title: Tissue: paper against power
steps.body:
Imtiaz Dharker was born in Pakistan and grew up in Glasgow. *Tissue* appeared in 2006. It is in copyright, so it is quoted here only in short phrases; read it in your anthology.

**Paper.** The poem is an extended metaphor. It begins with thin paper, “Paper that lets the light shine through”, and suggests “this is what could alter things”.

**What paper records.** Family names in the back of a Koran; maps, where “The sun shines through their borderlines”; receipts, “Fine slips from grocery shops” recording “what was paid by credit card”, which “might fly our lives like paper kites”. Human power is written on paper, and paper is fragile.

**What it could become.** The poem imagines an architect building with paper instead of brick, letting daylight through the shapes that pride makes.

**The ending.** The poem is in quatrains, and its last line stands alone: “turned into your skin”. Paper becomes human skin: we are as thin and as open to light.

visuals.alt: A table of four things paper stands for in Tissue and what each shows

check.prompt: Why does Dharker end Tissue with a single line after a poem of quatrains?
check.solution: After regular four-line stanzas the last line is alone. Breaking the structure breaks the control the poem questions, and leaves the reader with the image of paper turned into skin.

markScheme.description: The line stands alone and breaks the pattern, so its idea, paper as skin, is isolated and emphasised

options: Because the last line is the title
Because she ran out of space on the page and had to finish the poem quickly before the deadline for the collection, which is why the last stanza is shorter than the others
Because the poem is a sonnet
The line stands alone and breaks the pattern, so its idea, paper as skin, is isolated and emphasised

steps.title: Comparing Ozymandias and My Last Duchess
steps.body: Two powerful men, each allowed to speak, each undone by his words.

visuals.problem: Compare how power is presented in Ozymandias and My Last Duchess.

steps.text: Idea: both poems let absolute power speak for itself, and in both its words expose it.
Ozymandias speaks only through an inscription: “My name is Ozymandias, king of kings”, “Look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair!”.
steps.note: Power carved in stone, meant to last.

steps.text: The Duke speaks at length, and his words reveal a murder: “I gave commands; Then all smiles stopped together”.
steps.note: Power in conversation, meant to impress.

steps.text: Form: a sonnet that ends in empty desert, “The lone and level sands stretch far away”, against a monologue that ends on another possession, “Notice Neptune, though, Taming a sea-horse”.
steps.note: Time defeats one; the other goes on collecting.

steps.text: Judgement: Shelley shows power ended by time; Browning shows it still in force, choosing its next wife, which is more frightening.

visuals.alt: A table comparing Ozymandias and My Last Duchess by voice, form and ending

check.prompt: What is the key difference between the power in the two poems at their endings?
check.solution: Time has already defeated Ozymandias. The Duke is still in power, pointing out a bronze Neptune taming a sea-horse as he goes to discuss a dowry. The comparison shows two answers to what power becomes.

markScheme.description: Ozymandias's power is gone, buried in sand; the Duke's is still active, as he moves on to his next marriage

options: Ozymandias's power is gone, buried in sand; the Duke's is still active, as he moves on to his next marriage
Both men are dead at the end of their poems, killed by the people they ruled, which shows that Shelley and Browning both believed that tyrants are always overthrown by revolution in the end
Ozymandias is still alive and the Duke is dead
There is no difference

steps.title: Methods: voice and form
steps.body:
The four poems show four ways to give power a voice.

**Reported speech.** *Ozymandias* is a sonnet in which the king's words reach us third hand. The distance is the point: he is small now.

**First person, walking.** *London* is spoken by a man who wanders and hears. Four regular quatrains with an ABAB rhyme and heavy repetition sound like the city's routine.

**Dramatic monologue.** *My Last Duchess* is one long speech in rhyming couplets, but the sentences run over the line ends, so the rhyme is barely heard: the control is there, hidden under the talk, like the Duke's.

**Extended metaphor.** *Tissue* builds a single image through the whole poem, paper, and turns it at the end to skin.

visuals.alt: A table of the four poems with each form and its effect

check.prompt: Why might Browning run his sentences over the ends of his rhyming couplets?
check.solution: The couplets are strict, but enjambment makes the speech sound natural. Beneath the charm there is a rigid pattern, as beneath the Duke's manners there is absolute control.

markScheme.description: The rhyme's control is hidden under casual talk, as the Duke's cruelty is hidden under courtesy

options: Because the poem is written in prose
The rhyme's control is hidden under casual talk, as the Duke's cruelty is hidden under courtesy
To make the poem easier to sing
Because Browning did not know how to write rhyming couplets properly, and his editor corrected the poem after it was published in 1842, which is why some lines are longer than others

steps.title: Plan: London and Tissue
steps.body:
Try: *Compare how poets present the power of people or institutions over others in 'London' and in one other poem.* Choose *Tissue* as the second.

1. The idea that joins them: power written into things, streets, maps, receipts.
2. Voice: Blake's walking witness; Dharker's reflective speaker.
3. Imagery: manacles and a hearse; paper, maps and skin.
4. Form and ending: four heavy quatrains ending on the marriage hearse; quatrains ending on a single line.
5. Context: 1794 and the French Revolution; a poet between Pakistan and Scotland.

Then write the paragraph on imagery.

visuals.alt: Four boxes planning a comparison of London and Tissue

check.prompt: Which comparison of the two endings is strongest?
check.solution: The marriage hearse fuses love and death with no way out. Tissue's single last line is released from the stanza pattern and makes the reader's own skin the fragile paper. The comparison judges tone as well as image.

markScheme.description: Blake ends on a closed oxymoron, the marriage hearse; Dharker ends on an opening image, paper turned into skin, so one despairs and one hopes

options: Blake ends with a question and Dharker ends with an answer
Neither poem has an ending
Blake ends on a closed oxymoron, the marriage hearse; Dharker ends on an opening image, paper turned into skin, so one despairs and one hopes
Both poems end sadly because both poets thought that nothing could change in society, and both final lines describe a funeral taking place in a large city in Britain

steps.title: Context that explains the poem
steps.body:
Context earns AO3 marks when it explains a choice in a line.

**Shelley, 1818.** A radical in an age of kings. The sneer of cold command and the empty sand are a warning to rulers, including his own country's.

**Blake, 1794.** The French Revolution had begun in 1789; in Britain, radical writing was feared. “I wander through each chartered street” names ownership itself as the oppression.

**Browning, 1842.** The Victorian reader, living in a society where a wife was under her husband's authority, watches a husband's control carried to its end.

**Dharker, 2006.** A poet between countries writes of borders drawn on paper that the sun shines through.

Tie each to its line, one sentence each, inside the comparison.

check.prompt: Which context sentence works best for London?
check.solution: The sentence about the French Revolution ties a historical fact to a specific word and explains the choice. The others give facts with no link to a line.

options: William Blake was born in 1757 and died in 1827, and he was a painter and engraver as well as a poet, and he lived in London for most of his life in a number of different houses
Blake was a Romantic poet
London was a big city

steps.title: The power of humans in one page
steps.body:
Four poems about the power people hold over others, and what undoes it.

- **Ozymandias (Shelley, 1818):** a sonnet, reported; the boast and the empty sand; time defeats tyranny.
- **London (Blake, 1794):** a walker in a chartered city; every face marked; mind-forged manacles; the marriage hearse.
- **My Last Duchess (Browning, 1842):** a dramatic monologue; the curtain; I gave commands; the next wife.
- **Tissue (Dharker, 2006):** paper that lets the light through; maps, receipts, a holy book; paper turned into skin.
- **Methods:** reported voice, repetition, monologue, extended metaphor; form that contains or breaks.
- **Pairs:** Ozymandias with My Last Duchess; London with Tissue.

questions.prompt: Compare how poets present power in 'Ozymandias' and 'My Last Duchess'. Write the opening idea and one integrated paragraph on voice or ending.
questions.solution: Both poems let absolute power speak, and in both the words that were meant to impress expose it. Shelley gives his king only an inscription, “My name is Ozymandias, king of kings”; “Look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair!”, and reports it at third hand, through a traveller, so the voice that commanded a kingdom reaches us as a line in a story. Browning gives his Duke a whole poem, and the dramatic monologue lets him talk until he reveals what he did: “I gave commands; Then all smiles stopped together”. The endings show the difference. Ozymandias ends in “The lone and level sands stretch far away”: the power is gone. The Duke ends by drawing the envoy's attention to “Notice Neptune, though, Taming a sea-horse”, another possession, as he goes downstairs to arrange his next marriage. Shelley, a radical writing in 1818, could comfort his readers that time defeats tyrants; Browning, writing for Victorians who accepted a husband's authority over a wife, shows a tyranny that time has not touched, which makes his poem the more frightening of the two.

questions.prompt: Write one analytical paragraph on how Blake presents the power of institutions over people in 'London'.
questions.solution: Blake presents power as something built into the city and into people's minds. The speaker walks “I wander through each chartered street”, and the word *chartered*, meaning owned by legal charter, turns the streets and even the river into property. What he sees is uniform suffering: “Marks of weakness, marks of woe”, and the repetition of *every*, “In every cry of every man”, allows no exception. The cause is named in a metaphor: “The mind-forged manacles I hear”. The chains are forged in the mind, by fear, law and habit, so the people help to bind themselves. Then Blake names the institutions: the chimney-sweeper's cry makes “Every blackening church appals”, and “And the hapless soldier's sigh Runs in blood down palace-walls”, the soldier's blood a stain on the palace that sent him. The poem ends on an oxymoron, “And blights with plagues the marriage hearse”: even marriage carries death. Writing in 1794, when radical writing was feared in Britain after the French Revolution, Blake lays the blame on church, crown and the ideas that keep them in place.

how power works
context tied

The speaker walks “I wander through each chartered street”, and the word *chartered*, meaning owned by legal charter, turns the streets and even the river into property. What he sees is uniform suffering: “Marks of weakness, marks of woe”, and the repetition of *every*, “In every cry of every man”, allows no exception. The cause is named in a metaphor: “The mind-forged manacles I hear”. The chains are forged in the mind, by fear, law and habit, so the people help to bind themselves. Then Blake names the institutions: the chimney-sweeper's cry makes “Every blackening church appals”, and “And the hapless soldier's sigh Runs in blood down palace-walls”, the soldier's blood a stain on the palace that sent him. The poem ends on an oxymoron, “And blights with plagues the marriage hearse”: even marriage carries death. Writing in 1794, when radical writing was feared in Britain after the French Revolution, Blake lays the blame on church, crown and the ideas that keep them in place.

questions.prompt: A student writes: "Tissue is about tissue paper." What is the better account?
questions.solution: The literal paper opens into faith, maps, money, buildings and finally skin. The student has named the image and stopped before what it stands for.

markScheme.description: Paper is an extended metaphor for human power and life, fragile and open to light, ending as skin

options: The student is right: the poem describes the different kinds of tissue paper that can be bought in shops in Glasgow and Pakistan, and explains which kind is best for wrapping presents
Tissue is about a building
Paper is an extended metaphor for human power and life, fragile and open to light, ending as skin
Tissue is about a war

questions.prompt: Why does Browning never tell us directly what happened to the Duchess?
questions.solution: I gave commands; Then all smiles stopped together. The gap is the method: the reader fills it, and the Duke's calm makes it worse.

markScheme.description: The Duke's evasive words say it for him, and the reader's own conclusion is more chilling than a statement

options: Because the envoy interrupts
Because Browning did not know what had happened to the real Duchess of Ferrara, and he did not want to accuse the real Duke of murder in case his family sued him for libel
Because nothing happened to her
The Duke's evasive words say it for him, and the reader's own conclusion is more chilling than a statement

examTechnique.body:
**Know the voice of each.** Reported, witnessing, monologue, extended metaphor.

**Know the ending of each.** Endings are where the comparison is sharpest.

**Short, exact lines.** Especially for Tissue, which is not printed unless it is the named poem.

**Context in a sentence.** 1794 and the Revolution; 1818 and tyranny; 1842 and a husband's authority; 2006 and borders.
examinerErrors: Retelling what happens instead of analysing voice and form.
Treating Ozymandias as simply about a statue.
Missing the implication of I gave commands.
Writing about Tissue as literal paper.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer on these poems compares how power is given a voice and what undoes it. It reads the reported inscription, the witness's repetitions, the Duke's evasions and Dharker's extended metaphor as choices with effects, compares endings, and ties each poem's context to a line.
